name: Guduchi (Tinospora cordifolia)
short: Liver injury, including acute liver failure and hepatitis with autoimmune features, in 43 guduchi users in India (case series). A review of a 6-patient series and an essay blame other species.
text: In a retrospective study at 13 centres in India, 43 patients had herb-induced liver injury temporally associated with Tinospora cordifolia (guduchi, giloy) use, with a median of 46 days from first use to symptoms; they presented with acute hepatitis, acute worsening of chronic liver disease (the most common presentation) or acute liver failure, causality was rated probable in 67.4%, and the authors concluded that giloy is associated with acute hepatitis with autoimmune features and can unmask autoimmune hepatitis in people with silent autoimmune-related chronic liver disease. A case report describes a 50-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis who developed severely raised liver enzymes after starting a supplement containing Tinospora cordifolia, rated probable herb-induced liver injury on causality scoring; after the supplement was stopped and a three-day course of oral steroids, her enzymes returned to baseline within three months, and the authors describe the injury as appearing idiosyncratic and possibly immune-mediated. Two other articles, neither of whose abstracts names the 43-patient study, dispute that authentic T. cordifolia causes such injury: a review of an earlier case series of six patients with autoimmune-like hepatitis after guduchi use notes that Tinospora sinensis and Tinospora crispa are also traded as guduchi or giloy, that T. crispa is known to cause liver toxicity and that the botanical identity of the products in that series was not investigated, and concludes that authentic T. cordifolia is unlikely to have caused those patients' hepatitis and that a wrong species was probably taken; and an essay offering a counter-narrative to the research implicating giloy in drug-induced liver injury argues that clinical and toxicological evidence suggests guduchi is safe and attributes the observed harms to T. crispa. The multicentre study reports chemical and toxicological analyses of retrieved samples, but its abstract does not give their results. This evidence comes from case series and case reports rather than trials. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
